column4: Implementation of the Normalization Program in the Bangsamoro
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The Program for Normalization in the Bangsamoro, as provided in the Annex on Normalization, details the process whereby communities can achieve their desired quality of life, which includes the pursuit of sustainable livelihood and political participation within a peaceful deliberative society. It involves the transition of the decommissioned combatants to a peaceful and civilian life, redress of unresolved legitimate grievances and the rehabilitation of conflict-affected areas.

The four (4) main components of the Normalization process are as follows:

1. Security
- Policing
- Transitional security arrangements
- Decommissioning of MILF forces and weapons
- Redeployment of AFP units and troops
- Disbandment of private armed groups (PAGs)
- Management of Small Arms and Light Weapons 

2. Socio-economic Development 
- delivery of various socioeconomic development interventions to MILF decommissioned combatants, their families, and their communities 

3. Confidence-Building Measures
- provision of amnesty for MILF 
- development and transformation of the six previously-acknowledged MILF camps 

4. Transitional Justice and Reconciliation

column4: Philippine Anti-Illegal Drugs Strategy (PADS)
column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6:
PADS embodies a whole-of-nation approach that reinforces institutional and sectoral commitments to drug abuse prevention and control. It serves as a national framework designed to synchronize and strengthen all anti-illegal drug efforts. These include supply reduction measures, primarily through law enforcement and prosecution anchored in the rule of law and human rights, as well as demand reduction strategies such as prevention, rehabilitation, and reintegration. The strategy is further bolstered by robust international cooperation.

Aligned with the vision of the current administration, PADS seeks to sustainably intensify and streamline the government's anti-illegal drugs campaign within the framework of the law, with full respect for human rights, and a renewed emphasis on rehabilitation and socio-economic development. In support of this, the DILG is committed to advancing initiatives that promote public awareness, strengthen LGU participation, and encourage collaborative action among all sectors of society.

It also embodies the aspiration to ensure a secure and peaceful community where guns are silenced, food and basic services are sufficient, and community life has normalized and shown signs of progress. In the community, POC initiates, implements and monitors peace and order plans, programs, projects and activities that maintain peace and order in the locality. column4: Communities for Peace (C4Peace) Program
column5: Department of the Interior and Local Government
column6:
The Localization of Executive Order No. 70 Program Management Office (LEO70 PMO) was established in consonance with Executive Order No. 70 s. 2018, institutionalizing the whole-of-nation approach in attaining inclusive and sustainable peace, creating a national task force to end local communist armed conflict, and directing the adoption of a national peace framework.

In the updated Philippine Development Plan (PDP) 2023-2028, Chapter 13 “Ensuring Peace and Security and Enhance Administration of Justice,” specifically under Outcome 1: "Protection and development of conflict-affected communities sustained" which mentions the strategy to strengthen convergence programs and ensure development interventions are brought to geographically isolated and affected (GICA) communities. The Retooled Community Support Program (RCSP) is cited as a convergence mechanism for the implementation of the peace and development interventions.

Since 2019, the DILG has implemented the Communities for Peace (C4PEACE) Program (formerly known as Communicating for Perpetual End to Extreme Violence and Forming Alliance towards Positive Change and Enriched Communities from 2019-2023) to institutionalize the convergence of programs at the local level in support to the whole-of-nation and whole-of-government approach in ending local communist armed conflict. The program envisions LGUs to be at the forefront in bringing peace and development interventions through a more inclusive local development planning process. Community participation and involvement of immediate stakeholders is a highlight of the program.

The program is composed of the Retooled Community Support Program or RCSP for cleared barangays and the Capacitating Urban Communities for Peace and Development or CUCPD for cities and municipalities. Both programs encourage the participation of concerned stakeholders during consultations and dialogues to identify community/sectoral concerns. Inclusive local development planning is one of the major objectives of the program, wherein the program, projects, and activities of the LGUs are responsive to the needs of their constituents. The provision of capacity building interventions and delivery of basic services to far-flung areas are also strategies of the program to promote good governance.

column4: PAyapa at MAsaganang PamayaNAn (PAMANA) Program
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The PAMANA Program aims to contribute to (a) addressing issues of injustices and improve community access to socio-economic interventions; (b) improving governance by building the capacity of national government agencies (NGA) and local government units (LGU) for a conflict-sensitive, peace-promoting, culture-sensitive and gender-sensitive approach to human rights promotion and development; and, (c) empowering communities and strengthening their capacities to address issues of conflict and peace.
The PAMANA Program implementing framework is anchored on three (3) complementary strategic pillars that define core interventions to achieve just and lasting peace: (a) Pillar 1 - policy reform and governance interventions addressing issues on injustices relative to land security, natural resources, identity and human rights; b) Pillar 2 - capacity building interventions relative to strengthening government institutions and empowering communities; and, 3) Pillar 3 - peace promoting socio-economic interventions.
The PAMANA Program is one of the government's peace and development convergence programs for conflict-affected areas.

column4: Socio-economic Component for Individuals and Families of the Transformation Program for Moro National Liberation Front
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The peace process with the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) is a 46-year-old process, which started in the signing of the Tripoli Agreement in 1976 and the Final Peace Agreement (FPA) in 1996.

The 1996 FPA serves as the main policy framework of the Government in pursuing the implementation of individual and community-level interventions to deliver the peace dividends. However, the lack of provision on the management of forces and arms of the MNLF and the absence of a time-bound and targeted implementation of socio-economic packages to individuals and communities remain to be the challenges in completing the implementation of this Peace Agreement.

Hence, a transformation program of the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) was formulated as a parallel effort to the Normalization Program of the Moro Islamic Liberation Front (MILF) whereby communities can achieve their desired quality of life which includes the pursuit of sustainable livelihood and political participation within a peaceful deliberative society. It addresses the lack of provision on the management of forces and arms of the MNLF and the absence of a time-bound and targeted implementation of socio-economic packages to individuals and communities. It also intends to deter disgruntled MNLF combatants from joining the Abu Sayyaf Group and other violent extremist groups in Southern Philippines and avoid another “Zamboanga Siege” or “Marawi Siege”.

The interventions under the Transformation Program shall be aligned with the implementation of the larger transformation process in the Bangsamoro to include security, socio-economic development, confidence-building measures, community healing and reconciliation.

1.	Security Component

An Implementing Arrangements and Mechanisms on the Security Component of the MNLF Transformation Program was approved in October 2021 which serves as the guidelines in the full-scale implementation process of the validation, verification, and profiling of the MNLF combatants and firearms including the establishment of the Joint Body on Disposition of Arms and Forces (JBDAF) and related mechanisms to implement said processes. Once these processes are completed, the provision of socio-economic interventions for combatants, their families and communities shall commence.   

Validation is the process of comparing the list of MNLF members against the records on file from the Security Sector to identify qualified members for proper disposition and those with legal impediments that needs further assessment. On the other hand, Verification is process of positive identification of the combatants by his/her immediate commander and/or community leader as the person recorded in the submitted list while Profiling is the process to obtain the necessary information of the combatants that can be the basis for interventions such as socio-economic, confidence-building, and community healing and reconciliation.

JBDAF has been created to oversee the process of validation, verification and profiling of MNLF combatants, firearms and munitions under the purview of the GPH-MNLF Security Sub-Committee. Further, this mechanism is composed of (1) Joint Validation Team (JVAT) for the validation process; (2) Joint Verification Team (JVET) for the verification process; and (3) Joint Security Monitoring and Coordinating Team (JSMCT) for the overall security provision to the conduct of activities under the MNLF Transformation Program.

2.	Socio-economic Development Component 

It aims to provide stable livelihood and increase quality of life and condition of the combatants their families and communities. This will include livelihood opportunities, social protection packages and immediate cash assistance. 

Interventions for socio-economic will be done at three (3) levels: the individual combatant, his or her family and the community. 

The phases of socio-economic interventions are commensurate to the phases of the security component. Phase 1 shall be the delivery of initial socio-economic interventions such as transitional cash assistance, cash for work and civil registration as they transition from armed elements to civilians. This shall be provided to the combatants after the profiling process. On the other hand, Phase II of the socio-economic interventions shall be based on the needs assessment of each combatant which is part and parcel of the profiling process. The delivery of context-specific and tailor-fit interventions to the combatants and his or her family shall be done in exchange of the turn-in of the combatant’s firearms and ammunitions. While Phase III of the socio-economic interventions shall mainly focus on community-based interventions to ensure that the combatants and their families thrive in their own communities and the larger populace can also benefit from these interventions. This shall be commensurate to the destruction of firearms and munitions which shall still be subject for further discussion of the parties. 

3.	Confidence-building measures Component 

This component shall involve humanitarian and/or legal assistance that may be provided to the combatants and/or their next-of-kin. Community projects and interventions for vulnerable sectors of the community such as widows, orphans, persons with disabilities, and senior citizens are also included as confidence-building measures between the GPH and the MNLF.

One of the major programs under this component is the grant of Amnesty to MNLF members. On 5 February 2021, President Rodrigo Roa Duterte issued Executive Order 125 creating the National Amnesty Commission (NAC) and Proclamation 1091 granting amnesty to MNLF members, who have 	committed crimes in furtherance of their political beliefs. Pursuant to Executive Order 125 (s. 2021), the NAC shall be primarily tasked to receive and process applications for amnesty and to determine whether the applicants are entitled to amnesty under Proclamation 1091 (s. 2021), among others. It shall be composed of a Chairperson and two regular members to be appointed/designated by the President, and the Secretaries of the Department of Justice (DOJ), Department of National Defense (DND), Department of the Interior and Local Government (DILG), and the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation, and Unity (PAPRU) as ex-officio members.

4.	Healing and Reconciliation Component 

This component aims to enhance social cohesion, promote peacebuilding and contribute to peace and security in the communities where the MNLF are present. It shall have activities focused on the healing and reconciliation and bridging social divides, mainstreaming of conflict-sensitive and peace-promoting approaches in the delivery of individual and community packages and support programs and interventions of combatants, their families, and communities. 

The GPH and MNLF Sub-Committee on Community Healing and Reconciliation agreed on these elements that should be reflected in the framework and program for healing and reconciliation in MNLF communities.

- Addressing the hidden wounds of the past 
Psychosocial Healing program (counselling, grief management, therapy) for rebel returnees, families, trauma victims, and communities indirectly affected (profiling process may identify possible individuals who need help)	

- Acknowledgement and Surfacing Narratives. 1) Truth Telling Session / Listening Process with survivors and victims of violence from the war, 2) Commemoration / Remembrance of incidents of historical importance (e.g. Jabidah massacre, Malisbong massacre) as a way to honor those who lost their lives for the struggle and prevent recurrence.

- Forgiveness and Restoration of Relationships
Dialogues:  (a) between Muslim communities and the security sector and the local government (build trust and relationship) (b) with all sectors (popularization of narratives)
Education: Correcting narratives about Moros and including Muslim heroes in text books

column4: Preventing and Countering Violent Extremism and Insurgency (PCVEI)

In support of the whole-of-nation approach, the Department mobilizes its offices, bureaus, and attached agencies to collaborate with other NGAs, LGUs, and CSOs in addressing threats to national security. column4: Implementation of the Completion Strategy for the Cordillera Bodong Administration - Cordillera People's Liberation Army (CBA-CPLA) Peace Process
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The completion strategy for the CBA-CPLA Peace Process has a two-track approach. First, the Normalization Process of CBA-CPLA members and identified communities, with the overall objective of transformation into active partners for a peaceful and developing Cordillera Region free from CPP-NPA and other threats groups of the former CPLA combatants guided by the following principles:

Transform – support the transformation of the CBA-CPLA, building on gains since the 1986 Sipat. This will cover four levels of transformation: (i) individuals; (ii) CBA-CPLA as a former armed organization; (iii) communities supportive of the peace process; and (iv) their relationship with the Philippine Government and its instrumentalities- “From leaders of war to leaders of development and influential advocates of peace; meaningful participation in decision-making processes in their communities.”;

Sustain – sustain the gains of the Cordillera peace process by giving back to communities supportive to the CBA-CPLA; and,
Include – in the spirit of the Mt Data Sipat, support inclusive regional growth by prioritizing tribal communities that have lagged behind due to conflict and geographic isolation.

Consequently, the Normalization Program has four components namely: (i) Security; (ii) Socio-Economic Reintegration; (iii) Healing and Reconciliation; and (iv) Confidence Building. 
  
To support the intents, the Joint Evaluation and Monitoring Committee (JEMC) was created in December 2019 through OPAPP Office Order 197 that is tasked to establish a mechanism that will collate, discuss, analyze, and implement interventions for completing the commitments of the government for the CBA-CPLA Peace Process. 

Further, in consonance with the principle of honoring all signed peace agreements, the Government will continue to sustain programs and projects under the 2011 MOA, including the crafting of a 5-Year Partnership Strategy document. This document provides input into the socio-economic direction of the Normalization Program.  It also links to the 2011 MOA where policy actions, programs, projects, and activities should contribute to and complement the entire Cordillera Peace Process. 
  
The second approach is the provision of support to regional development advocacies towards helping the Cordillera Autonomy Bill be declared as a priority agenda of the Administration and is considered a common legislative agenda. 
  
To implement a consensus-based, multi-stakeholder Normalization Program to sustain the gains of the GPH-CBA-CPLA Peace Process, where the aspiration of the Cordillera People’s meaningful autonomy is supported, OPAPRU has provided CBA-CPLA members and families with agreed socio-economic interventions, access to basic services for CBA-CPLA identified communities.

column4: Completion of the 2000 Peace Agreement with the Rebolusyonaryong Partido ng Manggagawa-Pilipinas/Revolutionary Proletarian Army/Alex Boncayao Brigade (RPM-P/RPA/ABB)
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
Peace process with the RPM-P/RPA/ABB 

A.	Tabara-Paduano Group (TPG)

The Marcos Administration is pursuing the completion of the peace process with the RPM-P/RPA/ABB-TPG now known as “KAPATIRAN”, which was jumpstarted with the signing of the Clarificatory Implementing Document (CID) to the 2000 Peace Agreement between the Government and the RPM-P/RPA/ABB on 19 July 2019.  The completion strategy was initiated by the Administration of former President Rodrigo Roa Duterte with his directive to implement all signed peace agreements and being sustained by the Administration of President Ferdinand R. Marcos, Jr. anchored on the five-point peace, reconciliation and unity agenda.	

The 2019 CID lays down all the commitments between the GPH and the RPM-P/RPA/ABB-TPG and is part of the effort to achieve inclusive and sustainable peace in the country.  The CID has five components, namely: 1) Disposition of Arms and Forces and Security Arrangements, 2) Social and Economic Reintegration of the KAPATIRAN Members, 3) Release of the Remaining Alleged Political Offenders 4) Full transformation of the KAPATIRAN into a civilian organization engaging in socio-economic and political activities and, 5) Community Peace Dividends.  Originally envisioned to be implemented for three years from 2019 to 2022, the achievement of the commitments across the five CID components is projected to be attained by 2025, anchored on the multi-agency and local government convergence.  
The Transformation Roadmap for the KAPATIRAN will complete the committed interventions for the 727 members of the KAPATIRAN jumpstarted by the Government's execution of the 2019 CID as the final and absolute settlement of the 2000 GPH-RPM-P/RPA/ABB Peace Agreement. 

The Transformation Program Mechanisms that have been established are responsible in steering, monitoring and supervising the implementation of the CID components to bring to fruition the full transformation of the KAPATIRAN after two decades.   There are four mechanisms implementing mechanisms that have been organized to assist in the implementation of the 2019, namely:

1. Joint Enforcement and Monitoring Committee (JEMC), which supervises and monitors the implementation of the CID and will determine that all the objectives and commitments set forth by GPH and Tabara-Paduano Group/KAPATIRAN in the 2019 CID have been fulfilled;

2. Joint Body on the Disposition of Arms and Forces (JBDAF), which   is tasked to undertake regular security assessments, and provide updates and recommendations for appropriate action of the JEMC.

3. The eleven (11) Site Coordinating Teams (SCTs) in Western Visayas, which are  tasked to assist in implementing all the components of the 2019 CID as well as to ensure effective collaboration of agency commitments to the CID such as the establishment of settlement sites as peace and development community (PDC) and the provision of government social protection packages to KAPATIRAN members; and,

4. The 19-member Socio-Economic Reintegration Cluster (SERC), which is tasked to assist the JEMC in ensuring a holistic implementation of the provision of shelter and housing, land acquisition for congregated sites, and livelihood interventions to the KAPATIRAN. 

B.	Nilo Dela Cruz Group (NDCG)

The discussions with the NDCG is centered on the attainment of consensus towards completion of commitments within the framework of the 2000 Peace Agreement. Based on the meetings conducted, the following were identified:

The Release of Alleged Political Prisoners (APOs) and Political Prisoners (PPs), and Amnesty focuses on the review of the result of Civil and Political Rights (Annexes A, B, C, and the 144 List) and formulation of final list of remaining APOs/PPs as input to release and dropping of charges. Decommissioning pertains to the inventory and demilitarization of firearms, ammunition and explosives. The intent of the Reintegration Program is to prepare its members, especially those needing psychosocial preparation, prior to their re-entry to mainstream society and to be assisted through the implementation of Impact Development Projects. The Delivery of Impact Development Projects will begin with the identification of areas and beneficiaries, followed by conduct of community needs assessment, identification of projects (livelihood and area-based projects) and beneficiary assessment, the provision of capacity building (individuals and community), leading to resource delivery and project implementation and, finally, ensuring compliance and establishment of monitoring mechanisms (community-based).  Under Security Coordination Arrangement, regular updates and meetings will be conducted and, open communication with the security sector (AFP/PNP) shall be maintained. Policy reform and consultations with Rural Poor (farmers, fishermen, and farm workers), Urban Poor and Labor Sector were also discussed. And finally, the establishment of a JEMC for the NDCG.

column4: Critical Infostructure Evaluation and Cybersecurity Standards Monitoring Program
column5: Department of Information and Communications Technology
column6:
"The Critical Information Infrastructure (CII) Protection Program covers technical and
non-technical concerns and both organizational aspects must be given equal
importance. Understanding the CII protection risk management is necessary to ensure
the balanced approach to cover the cyber incident response cycle emphasized in the
NCSP 2028 (identify, contain, analyze, eradicate, recover, and learn). Thereafter is the
regular or systematic use of the risk management framework to strengthen and
implement the effective CII protection mechanisms/tools.

The major components of the CII Protection Program include:

1. Development and implementation of the CII Risk Management Framework
including its continuous assessment, updates and enhancements;
2. Identification of National Critical Infrastructure (NCI) and Critical Information
Infrastructure (CII);
3. Cybersecurity Compliance Evaluation and Monitoring Systems; and,
4. Establishment of National Cybersecurity Training and Research Center
(NCTRC).
5.The National Cyber Threat and Vulnerability Database Management System (NCTVDMS) is
an advanced knowledge based and response management system that logged all handled
cyber threats, attempts and incidents through system detected or reported from various
government agencies, critical information infrastructures sectors and businesses . The
historical information and lesson learned from the various handling experience performed by
CERT-PH and other cybersecurity government professionals who is involved in a specific cyber
incident including the containment, remediation and recovery steps will be carefully analyzed.
The information knowledge based can be utilized in the creation of incident prevention,
hardened configurations, mitigation and response management. The NCTVDMS will be
available to cybersecurity personnel from other government agencies and law enforcement
agencies as a shared and verified resource.
Beneficiaries:Government Agencies / Law Enforcement Agencies / Military / CIIs
6. The Philippine National Cyber Risk Assessment Program is build around the risk
management cycle that identifies risks and mitigations through interactive self
assessment, repeatable process and analysis of cyber risk which help the government
agencies and Critical Information Infrastructure to understand the nature of cyber risk
and methods to manage risk and kickstart cyber improvements identify strategic
investments.

column4: Mainstreaming Positive Peace towards Local Development Program
column6:
The attainment of just and lasting peace is critical to the realization of AmBisyon Natin 2040 or the Filipino people’s collective aspiration of a matatag, maginhawa, at panatag na buhay. Peaceful communities can harness the fruits of economic growth through improved access to government services and financial opportunities, and increased overall human development, without fear or threat to lives and livelihoods. This perspective is a reflection of the significant strides towards the understanding of peace and development over many decades.

In 1953, Martin Luther King wrote about ‘negative peace’ as the absence of tension and ‘positive peace’ as the presence of justice. This concept was introduced into academic literature by the Norwegian peace researcher, Johan Galtung, defining ‘positive peace’ as the attitudes, institutions, and structures (systems) that create and sustain peace, able to gauge the resilience of a society or its ability to absorb shocks without falling or relapsing into conflict. 

In line with this, the positive peace systems thinking approach can be seen reflected in policies such as Executive Order No. 70 s. 2018 ‘Institutionalizing the Whole-of-Nation Approach in Attaining Inclusive and Sustainable Peace, Creating a National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), and Directing the Adoption of the National Defence Framework,’ the DILG’s Memorandum Circular 2020-095 ‘Remedial Measures on the Localization of RO No. 70 and all DILG Peacebuilding Activities’ as well as programs such as the Department’s Capacitating Urban Communities Program (CUCPD), Retooled Community Support Program (RCSP), and other national-level programs such as the Support to Barangay Development Program (SBDP).

As the mandated agency for the capacity development (CapDev) of both local government units (LGUs) and DILG Personnel, LGA remains committed to providing excellent and innovative training solutions to its clients and the harmonization of CapDev for LGUs. This program, anchored on the concepts of Positive Peace, intends to build on the gains of other nationally-implemented peace and development programs by raising awareness and creating a common understanding of peace and development across all local communities.

column4: Security Component of the Transformation Program for the Moro National Liberation Front
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The Transformation Program for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) is rooted in the socioeconomic provisions of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement. The Transformation Program for MNLF combatants, their families, and communities was developed through consultations with MNLF groups. Its primary goal is to support the transition of MNLF members from armed combatants to peaceful, productive civilians, while also preventing recruitment into violent extremist groups. The program is structured into three key phases to ensure a smooth and sustainable reintegration of MNLF combatants into civilian life. 

The first phase, Settling-In and Transition, focuses on providing immediate support through transitional safety nets for combatants and their families, helping them adjust to life beyond armed struggle. This is followed by the Transforming for the next stage phase, which aims to uplift their socio-economic conditions through sustainable livelihood assistance and other development interventions. Finally, the Stabilizing phase seeks to organize combatants into collective identities, fostering social cohesion, unity, and long-term stability within their communities.
The Program is anchored on four key components:
Security component – Focuses on the inventory and verification of firearms and ammunition, in coordination with the AFP and PNP.

column4: Community Healing and Reconciliation Component for the Transformation Program of Moro National Liberation Front
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
The Transformation Program for the Moro National Liberation Front (MNLF) is rooted in the socioeconomic provisions of the 1996 Final Peace Agreement. Aimed at achieving lasting and sustainable peace in Southern Philippines, particularly in Mindanao, the program primarily benefits MNLF former combatants, their families, and their communities. It consists of two primary tracks: The Political Track and the Socioeconomic Track. Within the Socioeconomic Track, four major components are emphasized: security, socioeconomic development, the amnesty program, and community healing and reconciliation.

The framework and program of this component is undergoing enhancement through the GPH-MNLF subcommittee level. This year, the subcommittee has programmed to implement initial interventions in communities with experiences of conflict to address trauma and developmental challenges. 

Preparations are also underway to support the capacity-building component of the Ministry of Social Services and Development’s Bangsamoro Sagip Kabuhayan Program wherein 3,000 MNLF women under the leadership of Chair Nur Misuari are expected to benefit from seed capital amounting to PhP 15,000.00 per beneficiary.  Upcoming capacity-building activities will focus on project management, peacebuilding, and basic financial management.

For this year’s observance of Ramadan, solidarity activities through Iftars or breaking of the fast were held in six (6) MNLF communities to foster social healing and unity. Women conversations preceded the events, highlighting their roles during Ramadan, their needs, and community concerns, alongside a brief orientation on Women, Peace, and Security. Here are the communities benefitting from these activities for the last 3 years.

column4: Five-Year Acquisition of Mission Essential Equipment Plan of NSWF
column6:
NSWF will be equipped with shoulder-launched anti-armor and anti-air systems—lightweight, man-portable launchers designed for single-operator use against armored vehicles, fortified positions, and low-flying aircraft. These disposable or reusable systems can employ a range of warheads and, in modern variants, incorporate optional guided munitions and advanced sighting solutions to enhance precision during maritime interdiction, boarding actions, or shore operations.

To complement this firepower, operators will also employ closed-circuit rebreather systems that greatly improve underwater stealth, endurance, and operational reach during clandestine maritime missions. By recycling breathing gas and eliminating visible exhalation bubbles, rebreathers reduce acoustic and visual signatures while enabling multi-hour dive profiles far longer than those achievable with open-circuit systems. Contemporary units integrate electronic oxygen monitoring, CO₂ scrubbers, automatic gas-mix management, and heads-up displays for critical alerts, and their modular, lightweight construction supports use with diver helmets, mixed-gas profiles, and swimmer delivery vehicles across a wide range of marine environments.

column4: National Peace Engagement
column5: Office of the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation and Unity
column6:
Since the termination of formal peace negotiations on 23 November 2017, the Government of the Philippines (GPH) and the National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDFP) have gradually reopened channels for dialogue. From June 2022 to August 2023, a series of exploratory meetings was conducted to reassess the prospects for peace. These efforts culminated in the signing of a Joint Statement on 23 November 2023, wherein both Parties reaffirmed their shared commitment to a principled and peaceful resolution of the armed conflict. Resolving the roots of the armed conflict and ending the armed struggle shall pave the way for the transformation of the CPP-NPA-NDFP. (See Annex A for a copy of the Joint Statement)

In line with this development, the Presidential Adviser on Peace, Reconciliation, and Unity (PAPRU) briefed the President and sought approval to continue the exploratory talks, which enabled the Parties to progress toward the drafting of a Framework Agreement, which serves as a guiding document/outline for the Comprehensive Peace Agreement.

On 26 March 2025, during the 7th Executive Committee Meeting of the National Task Force to End Local Communist Armed Conflict (NTF-ELCAC), President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. sought updates on the ongoing exploratory talks between the GPH and the CPP-NPA-NDF, expressing interest in how the process can be sustained toward the conclusion of a Comprehensive Peace Agreement. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. was provided with updates on the ongoing exploratory efforts by the OPAPRU, emphasizing that the initiative is not a continuation of past negotiations, but a completely fresh start – a “clean sheet” approach. (See Annex B, letter f and g under #2, of the After-Activity Report of the 7th Executive Committee on 26 March 2025)

Parallel to the ongoing exploratory talks, a series of orientation sessions and consultations have been undertaken to ensure that the proposed Framework Agreement reflects a broad range of perspectives and is anchored within the Philippine Constitution. These activities engaged internal stakeholders, such as national agencies and local government units, as well as external stakeholders, including church organizations. Notably, targeted engagements were conducted with the security sector, whose strategic involvement is essential given their operational role and influence on peace and security outcomes.

column4: Development of Modern Specialized BFP Training Facility
column6:
The Development of Modern Specialized BFP Training Facility
involves the construction, equipping, and operationalization of a
state-of-the-art regional training center that will cater to BFP
personnel from the provinces and cities within Region 10 and other regions within Mindanao. The
The facility will include training facilities, classrooms, and support
structures, ensuring realistic and safe training conditions for
diverse emergency scenarios.

Currently, the absence of a modern regional training facility limits
the conduct of standardized training, resulting in unequal
competency levels across local stations. The project will address
this gap by localizing capacity-building programs, reducing
dependence on national training centers, and improving
operational efficiency and response capability.

Implementation will be undertaken by the BFP Region 10
Regional Office, following standard government procurement
processes and existing modernization guidelines. The project will
engage potential partners from academic institutions, LGUs, and
emergency response organizations to promote knowledge
exchange, technical collaboration, and program accreditation.
This approach will ensure the facility operates as a center of
excellence for firefighter training, innovation, and regional
cooperation.

column4: Satellite Off-Campus Fire Training Institute in Ubay, Bohol
column6:
The establishment of the Bureau of Fire Protection (BFP) Regional Fire Training Center in 
Bohol is a strategic initiative aimed at enhancing fire service training and strengthening 
emergency response capabilities in Region VII. As part of the BFP’s nationwide effort to 
decentralize firefighter education, this facility will serve as a dedicated training hub, ensuring 
that personnel across the region receive standardized, high-quality instruction in fire
suppression, rescue operations, and disaster response. While the primary training center for 
the Fire Basic Recruitment Course (FBRC) is located at Camp Vicente Lim in Laguna, the 
increasing demand for well-trained firefighters has led to the expansion of regional training 
centers. In 2023, BFP Region 10 successfully inaugurated a satellite Fire Training Institute in 
Impasug-ong, Bukidnon, catering to fire service personnel in Mindanao. Following this model,
Bohol has been identified as the next location for a regional training center to serve firefighters 
from Central Visayas.
